title: Drones are the largest driver of defence industry battery demand
gist: Drones have become the single largest driver of military battery demand, rising from 20% to 39.2% of defence battery demand between 2020 and 2025, with the supply chain currently anchored by China's vertically integrated drone-and-battery industry — a structural chokepoint Benchmark expects to deepen as China's share of global defence battery demand exceeds 50% by 2035.

themes.theme: Drones now dominate defence battery demand

insights.claim: Drones accounted for 39.2% of defence demand for batteries in 2025, up from just 20% in 2020, making them the largest single driver of military battery demand.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Battery demand forecasting for the defence sector should now be modeled primarily around drone program growth rather than legacy platforms; a near-doubling of share in five years implies a steep further trajectory.
insights.locator: In 2025, drones accounted for 39.2% of defence demand

insights.claim: After drones, soldier power systems and military bases are the next two largest drivers of defence battery demand.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Identifies the secondary demand pools worth tracking alongside drones for battery suppliers targeting the defence vertical.
insights.locator: Soldier power and bases are the two next largest drivers

insights.claim: Major militaries are still only in the early stages of their strategic investment in drone-related battery supply chains, which is expected to trigger a surge of activity to domesticate those supply chains among both established battery manufacturers and new entrants.
insights.speaker: Will Roberts
insights.so_what: A coming wave of domestication investment is a direct opportunity signal for battery manufacturers and new entrants positioning in defence-linked supply chains, particularly outside China.
insights.quote: Major militaries are still just getting started in their strategic investments relating to them which is about to set off a flurry of activity to domesticate supply chains, something which is getting significant attention from major battery manufacturers and new entrants alike.

themes.theme: China's chokepoint on drone and battery supply chains

insights.claim: China has the world's largest and most vertically integrated drone industry, combining dominant manufacturing capacity with the deepest component supply chain, including for batteries.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: China's vertical integration across drones, batteries, and critical minerals means any non-Chinese drone program faces a structural cost and speed disadvantage without a domestic alternative supply chain.
insights.locator: China has the world's largest and most vertically integrated drone industry

insights.claim: Modern drone warfare, including in Ukraine, remains deeply reliant on Chinese-origin inputs across upstream critical minerals, batteries and magnets, creating chokepoints where a supply disruption could have immediate battlefield consequences.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Frames Chinese input dependency as a live battlefield risk, not just a commercial one — any Chinese export restriction on these inputs would have near-term military effects, a scenario worth monitoring for escalation risk.
insights.locator: As a result, modern drone warfare, including in Ukraine

insights.claim: The US and Europe face a significant challenge in reducing reliance on Chinese battery and drone supply chains without undermining their own ability to scale production.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Highlights a real trade-off facing Western defence-industrial policy: de-risking from China too fast could slow their own drone production scale-up, a tension relevant to defence procurement and industrial policy bets.
insights.locator: These chokepoints create a structural vulnerability

themes.theme: Shifting regional demand: Europe now, China by 2035

insights.claim: Europe is currently the largest driver of defence battery demand, driven by Ukraine's rapid adoption of drone technology.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Points to the Ukraine conflict as the current epicenter of defence battery demand growth, relevant for suppliers assessing near-term order flow.

insights.claim: Benchmark forecasts that China will grow to account for over half of global defence battery demand by 2035 as it accelerates deployment of drones in its own military activities.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: A long-run forecast that defence battery demand leadership shifts from Europe to China over the next decade — a signal for where future defence-linked battery capacity investment may concentrate and for the geopolitical stakes of that concentration.

insights.claim: Batteries have shifted from being viewed primarily as an energy transition story to being equally a defence and security story, sitting at the heart of modern military capability from drones to soldier power systems and making battery supply chains a focal point of the geopolitical contest between the US and China.
insights.speaker: Brayn Bille
insights.so_what: Reframes battery supply chains as dual-use critical infrastructure subject to national-security policy (export controls, subsidies, stockpiling), which materially changes the risk and opportunity calculus for battery investors versus a pure clean-energy framing.
insights.quote: Batteries were once seen as an energy transition story. Today, they are just as much a defence and security story. From drones to soldier power systems, batteries now sit at the heart of modern military capability — making them a critical dual-use technology and placing battery supply chains squarely in the geopolitical crossfire between the US and China.
